items.alt: Bilar man-made forest along the Loay Interior Road

children.text: A signature Philippine landscape of 1,200 to 1,700-odd cone-shaped limestone hills rising across about 50 km² in the middle of Bohol Island. In the dry season, the grass dries out and the hills turn chocolate-brown; a viewpoint and ATV rides let you experience them up close.

The Chocolate Hills are a cluster of cone-shaped hills scattered across Carmen, Batuan, and Sagbayan in central Bohol. Depending on the counting method, the hills number anywhere from 1,268 to 1,776, rising across about 50 km², mostly
tall, with the highest exceeding

. They look as if someone had scattered giant chocolate kisses across the grassland, and this signature Philippine scene appears without fail on the back of the 200-peso bill and in tourism promotions.

The hills are explained as karst terrain: coral reef and limestone that piled up on an ancient seabed were later uplifted, and over long ages, rain and groundwater eroded them until only the hardest parts remained as cones. Almost no trees grow on the hills, only grass, so they're green in the rainy season but turn brown when the grass dries out in the dry season — the source of the "chocolate" name. Local legend also tells of boulders thrown by two feuding giants, or of hardened tears shed by a giant named Arogo over an unrequited love.
The Chocolate Hills were designated a National Geological Monument in
, and when the whole of Bohol Island was recognized in
as the Philippines' first UNESCO Global Geopark (the Bohol Island Geopark), they became its centerpiece attraction. In
, a resort built among the hills drew nationwide attention over a protected-area controversy.
The best-known viewing site, the Chocolate Hills Complex, is in Barangay Buenos Aires in Carmen, about
55km

by road from Tagbilaran, the provincial capital of Bohol. Geologically, it is classified as "cockpit karst," terrain formed when marine limestone laid down in the late Pliocene to early Pleistocene (a layer mixed with marine fossils) was dissolved and eroded by rainwater. Presidential Proclamation No. 1037 of
July 1, 1997
placed the area under protection and specified the number of hills as 1,776, and in
it was included among the protected areas under the Expanded National Integrated Protected Areas System Act (E-NIPAS, Republic Act No. 11038). The magnitude 7.2 Bohol earthquake of
October 15, 2013
badly damaged the viewpoint and its facilities, and after restoration costing about
it reached its present form.

The visit itself centers on climbing to the viewpoint for the view, so an hour or two is enough, but most travelers combine it into a "countryside tour" for the day along with the Tarsier Sanctuary, the Loboc River cruise, and Baclayon Church. It's a must on the itinerary for families with children, a filial trip with parents, or anyone visiting Bohol for the first time.
About 214 steps cut into one of the hills at the Chocolate Hills Complex take you up to a view of hills stretching endlessly in every direction. The stairs are steep but climbable in about
10 minutes

blocks.title: Riding an ATV between the hills

children.text: ATV operators near the viewpoint run courses along dirt paths between the hills. A
30-minute to 1-hour
course is typical, and since mud gets splattered, wear clothes you don't mind getting dirty.

This activity park (CHAP) is in Sitio Camanayon of the same Barangay Buenos Aires as the viewpoint, and offers a bike zipline and a surfboard-style zipline that cross between the hills, a treetop rope course, and mountain biking. Admission is about
and the bike zipline is about
. Each activity is priced separately, so check the signboards on site.

blocks.title: Hill scenery along the Loay Interior Road

children.text: At the end of the Loay Interior Road, which runs past Bilar and on to Carmen, the hills press in close on both sides of the road. If you've chartered a vehicle, stop briefly on a safe shoulder to photograph the hills from a different eye level than the viewpoint.

blocks.title: Drive through the Bilar mahogany forest

children.text: On the road from Tagbilaran to the Chocolate Hills, Bilar has about
2km
of densely planted mahogany trees forming a man-made forest — a good spot to pull over briefly for photos.

blocks.title: Combine it into a countryside tour

children.text: It's most efficient to see the Blood Compact Shrine, Baclayon Church, the Tarsier Sanctuary, and the Loboc River lunch cruise together with the Chocolate Hills in a single day.
Near closing time, the low sun casts long shadows across each hill, producing more three-dimensional photos than at midday.

blocks.title: Viewpoint complex facilities and time needed

children.text: The viewpoint complex is built around a climb of about 214 steps, with a rest pavilion partway up and a two-level deck at the top. The complex has a café, a souvenir shop, and restrooms, and many travelers spend
1–2 hours
here taking photos. Every facility requires climbing the stairs, so strollers and wheelchairs are not practical.

It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes

from Manila to Bohol–Panglao International Airport (TAG), with daily flights from Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and others. Direct flights from Incheon, Korea, to Bohol also operate, though this varies by airline and season. From the airport to the Chocolate Hills is about
1.5–2 hours
by car.
Fast craft such as OceanJet run several times daily from Cebu to Tagbilaran Port; the trip takes about
2 hours
, with fares of about
depending on seat class.
From the Dao Integrated Bus Terminal in Tagbilaran, a bus to Carmen takes about
1.5–2 hours
and costs about
. Just tell the driver to drop you off on the road in front of the viewpoint entrance; from the entrance to the viewpoint the road climbs, so a habal-habal (about
) is easier. Buses back run less frequently in the late afternoon.
Weesam Express, Lite Ferries, FastCat, and other operators run from Cebu City to Tubigon Port on the northwest coast of Bohol. The trip takes about
1–2 hours
depending on the operator, and fares are about
by seat class; a fuel surcharge can push them above the listed fare. From Tubigon Port to Carmen takes about
1 hour
by multicab or bus (about
) or by van (about
), though buses make many stops and can take longer. Timetables differ by operator and change often, so check before you depart.
The most comfortable option is to charter a van or car for the day and do the countryside tour. Starting from Panglao, a car runs about
, with entrance fees and meals usually extra. Many travelers rent their own motorbike, but it's a one-way mountain drive of about
60km
, so you should have riding experience.
From Carmen town to the viewpoint complex takes about
10 minutes
by habal-habal or tricycle. Before

, private cars and motorbikes can drive up and park near the top of the complex, but after that the usual arrangement is to park in the roadside lot along the highway and take the free shuttle. The arrangement changes with the season, so follow the instructions on site.
If you rent a motorbike, just search for "Chocolate Hills Complex" on Google Maps and navigate there. A day's rental is about
, and since there are many uphill stretches, a 125cc or larger model is recommended. Avoid driving mountain roads before dawn or at night.
The hills take on their namesake chocolate color mainly during the drier
late February to May
April–May
especially sees the grass dry out the most for a deep brown, but midday temperatures can top 33°C, so an early-morning visit is best.
June–January
is the rainy season and its aftermath, when the hills stay green — the green hills have their own beauty, and the clear air makes for sharp photos.
Bohol sits on the southern edge of the Philippine typhoon path, so it's less affected than Luzon, but
October–December
can bring low-pressure systems and heavy rain that make mountain roads slippery and turn the ATV course muddy. Around the third week of
July
, when the Sandugo Festival is held across Bohol, Tagbilaran gets crowded.
Bohol has no pronounced dry season, so the color of the hills depends more on that year's rainfall than on the calendar. Even in the same
April

, if it has rained often, some green can remain, so it's safer to check recent visitors' photos before you set out to see the current color. Even in the dry season there are many cloudy days, so leave some slack on site to wait for the sky to open up. The town of Carmen holds its town fiesta on the feast day of St. Anthony Abbot on
January 17
, and during Holy Week (late March to early April) and the year-end holidays, more domestic tourists come and the viewpoint stairs get crowded.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Since the Chocolate Hills are usually a day trip, accommodation is generally booked on Panglao Island (around Alona Beach) or in Tagbilaran city. Beachfront resorts on Panglao run about
or more a night, and Tagbilaran city hotels run about
. If you want quiet countryside scenery, another option is to spend a night at a riverside or mountain lodge near Loboc or Bilar and see the Chocolate Hills early the next morning.

Near the viewpoint there are souvenir shops and a few simple restaurants, but options are limited, so many countryside tours handle lunch with the Loboc River cruise buffet. Bohol specialty snacks such as calamay (a chewy rice cake served in coconut husks), ube (purple yam) desserts, and piaya are popular souvenirs to buy.

The café in the viewpoint complex sells Filipino home-style dishes such as chicken adobo, sisig (a sizzling plate of chopped pork), and pancit, along with drinks. The menu is limited, so on a countryside tour it's usual to have lunch at the Loboc River buffet cruise (about
). If you're getting there on your own, bring water and snacks from your hotel; Carmen town has few places to stay, so a day trip from Panglao or Tagbilaran is the easy choice.
It's best to assume there's no ATM near the viewpoint. Prepare cash for entrance fees, the ATV, and snacks.
Arriving around
lets you climb the stairs before the tour groups arrive. There's almost no shade at midday, and it gets very hot.
It's windy at the top of the viewpoint, so wear a hat with a strap, and check on-site rules before flying a drone.
ATV operators vary in course and duration, so confirm and negotiate "how many minutes to which viewpoint" — most include photo stops.
When booking a countryside tour, be sure to confirm whether the entrance fee and the Loboc cruise are included, and the pickup time.
Phone signal generally reaches near the viewpoint but is weak through the Bilar forest section.
Popular photo compositions are looking down at the hills from partway up the stairs, and the hills beyond the rice paddies along the ATV course.
The viewpoint complex is generally open from
8:00 AM to 5:30 PM
. Since
October 1, 2025
admission has risen to
for adults not resident in Bohol and
for Bohol residents and children aged 6–12; children 5 and under are free, and only cash is accepted.
Whether senior citizen and persons-with-disability discounts apply is unclear because sources describe it differently. If you qualify, bring your ID and check at the ticket booth.

Countryside tours usually cover Loboc and the tarsiers in the morning and reach the Chocolate Hills in the afternoon, so you hit the midday heat and the tour groups together. When booking, ask whether the Chocolate Hills can be visited first.
The complex has restrooms, a café, and a souvenir shop. Use the restroom before climbing the stairs, and travel light.
Climbing onto the hills or digging into their soil violates protected-area rules. Do not leave the viewpoint or the designated ATV course.
The viewpoint stairs are steep and slippery when wet. Anyone with weak knees should climb slowly and hold the railing.
ATVs occasionally roll over. Wear a helmet, follow behind the guide, and have children ride in a car with a guide.
Entrance fees and operating rules have changed under municipal ordinances over time. Check the latest notices from the Carmen municipal government or the Bohol tourism office before visiting.
Midday sun is very strong, so be sure to bring water, sunscreen, and a hat.
The Sagbayan Peak viewpoint to the north has been closed since around
April 2025
for violating commercial operation rules. Even if it appears in older tour guides or maps, check whether it has reopened before visiting.
In the dry season the grass on the hills dries out completely, and in
April 2024
grass fires broke out on two of the hills. Never throw away cigarettes or embers at the viewpoint or on the ATV trails.
Successive typhoons in late
(Tino, Uwan, and Verbena) damaged part of the access road to the viewpoint, and repair work began in
January 2026
(a construction period of about
81 days
). The access road has no walkway, so pedestrians and vehicles easily share the same space; take care when walking, and check the road condition before you visit.
In
October 2025

the government moved to close about 500 small businesses operating inside the protected area without an Environmental Compliance Certificate (ECC), but halted the effort after pushback. The way nearby ATV operators and shops do business may change, so check the latest news.
